opus-5.5.text:
I think the signal was already there by early 2025, and honestly a lot of teams, including people I respect, were a bit slow to read it.

AIME was a very good benchmark for one specific phase. When reasoning models first appeared, we needed a clean, verifiable target to prove that reinforcement learning on long chains of thought actually worked. Math competition problems were perfect: the answer is right or wrong, the reward is unambiguous, and you can see the model learning to reflect, backtrack, and verify itself. So pushing AIME scores was a meaningful way to validate the paradigm.

But once multiple teams reached roughly the same high level, the marginal gain from another few points became very small, both scientifically and for users. That's the first judgment criterion I'd use: **when a benchmark stops differentiating what the model can actually do in the world, it has finished its job.** If going from 80 to 88 on AIME doesn't change anything for someone trying to get real work done, you are optimizing a proxy, not the capability.

The second signal is where the bottleneck moves. Reasoning in a closed box, one question, one answer, is mostly solved in the sense that the model can think for a long time and get there. The hard problems are now open-ended: the model has to call tools, read an environment, recover from errors, keep a goal across many steps, and decide when it's done. Those abilities don't show up on AIME at all. You can have a model that's brilliant at olympiad math and still falls apart in a twenty-step coding task because it loses track of context or can't handle a messy tool output.

The third thing is infrastructure, and I think this is what really determined who moved early. Agentic RL needs very different systems: environments, sandboxes, long rollouts, asynchronous training, reward design for tasks that aren't simply right or wrong. If you wait until benchmarks fully saturate before building that, you're already behind, because the infrastructure takes months. So the right timing was not "when AIME is maxed out," it was "as soon as we're confident the reasoning recipe works, start building the agent stack in parallel."

So my view is: treat AIME as a milestone that proves the method, then shift resources quickly. The teams that did well were the ones willing to give up a bit of leaderboard glory to invest in something harder to measure but much closer to how people will actually use these models.

r001.rationale: The response describes AIME as a useful validation benchmark and gives an illustrative 80-to-88 example, but it does not identify a score around 60–70 as evidence that the existing pipeline is working.

r002.rationale: It says the signal was present by early 2025 and recommends starting to build the agent stack in parallel as soon as the reasoning recipe works, then shifting resources quickly.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most teams, including ours, didn't make that call through some clean analysis. We made it when the benchmark stopped telling us anything new.

By early 2025, AIME had become a kind of mirror. You trained on reasoning data with RL, you pushed the score up, and everyone cheered. But the signal flattened very quickly. When several labs are all within a few points of each other on a competition math set, the marginal point no longer reflects a real capability gap. It reflects data curation, prompt format, sometimes contamination. The moment I remember clearly was looking at an internal dashboard where our score went up and our own researchers weren't more productive with the model. That gap between the number and the lived experience is the signal to leave.

So if I had to turn it into a judgment principle, I'd say three things. First, ask whether the benchmark still discriminates between models that users actually experience as different. If it doesn't, you're optimizing a proxy that has detached from the target. Second, look at where the failures of your best model actually live. In 2025 the failures weren't in solving a hard problem in one pass. They were in long horizons: the model lost track of state, it couldn't recover from its own mistakes, it didn't know when to go check something. None of that shows up on AIME, and all of it shows up the moment you give the model a terminal and a task that takes forty steps. Third, watch what your own people reach for. Once engineers start wiring the model into loops with tools, memory, and verification by themselves, the architecture question has already been answered for you, and the only remaining question is whether you build it properly or let it grow as a pile of scripts.

I'd also add a caution, because I don't think the shift should have been a clean break. The reasoning work wasn't wasted. A model that can't sustain a long chain of inference falls apart as an agent anyway, because an agent is really just reasoning stretched across time and interrupted by the world. The teams that did this well kept the reasoning training and changed what they measured: task completion over many steps, recovery rate after an error, cost per solved task. The teams that did it badly either kept chasing the leaderboard six months too long, or abandoned reasoning research entirely and ended up with agent frameworks around a model that couldn't think.

So the timing wasn't about a date. It was about recognizing when your evaluation had become theater, and having the courage to replace it with something messier that actually hurt to look at.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AIME scores had flattened and no longer reflected real capability, but gives no score of roughly 60–70 or claim that such a score showed the pipeline was working.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes shifting toward agent architectures when benchmarks stop being useful, but gives no mid-2025 timing and says the shift should not be a clean break.

astra-6.text:
I think the signal should have been the gap between benchmark progress and what the system could actually do. AIME is useful for measuring a certain kind of reasoning. But if your score keeps improving while your model still struggles to use tools, recover from mistakes, or finish a task over many steps, then that score is no longer enough to guide the team.

I would have wanted a parallel effort: keep improving reasoning, but test it inside an agent loop. Can the model recognize that an action failed? Can it change its plan based on new information? Can it complete the task reliably, at an acceptable cost? Those tests help you understand whether the bottleneck is the model, the training, or the architecture around it.

So I wouldn’t choose a particular month in 2025 as the turning point. I would shift investment when another improvement on AIME stopped translating into better task completion, and experiments with agent architectures showed a more promising path. You need to start those experiments early enough to have evidence when you make that decision.

sol-6.1.text:
I would have treated that as a question about what the scores were still teaching us. If an improvement on AIME translated into better reasoning across unfamiliar tasks, it was valuable. But if the score kept rising while the model still struggled to use tools, recover from mistakes, or complete a long task, then the benchmark was no longer telling us enough about the next bottleneck.

For agents, the unit of evaluation has to become the whole task. Can the system choose an action, interpret the result, revise its plan, and finish with a verifiable outcome? And can it do that at an acceptable cost and latency?

So I wouldn’t have made it a single switch in 2025. I would have run both efforts in parallel and shifted resources as the evidence changed. If stronger reasoning stopped improving end-to-end completion, while changes to the agent architecture did improve it, that would have been the signal to invest more heavily in the architecture.
